title: Chapter LIV

teacherSummary.text: At dinner Bingley sits by Jane. Darcy is distant and seated far from Elizabeth. Jane claims she and Bingley are only friends; Elizabeth doubts it.

vocabulary.definition: Any one of numerous species of small gallinaceous birds of the genus Perdix and several related genera of the family…
vocabulary.context: Darcy acknowledged, that the partridges were remarkably well done; and I suppose he has two or three French cooks at least.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “partridge”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Bennet had designed to keep the two Netherfield gentlemen to supper; but their carriage was unluckily ordered before any of the others, and she had no opportunity of detaining them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “detain”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + tain (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To give strength or ability to
vocabulary.context: She was in hopes that the evening would afford some opportunity of bringing them together; that the whole of the visit would not pass away without enabling them to enter into something more of conversation, than the mere ceremonious salutation attending his entrance.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “enable”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The venison was roasted to a turn—and everybody said they never saw so fat a haunch.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “venison”: ven (Latin venire, "to come"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To cook by exposure to radiant heat before a fire
vocabulary.context: The venison was roasted to a turn—and everybody said they never saw so fat a haunch.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “roast”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: She followed him with her eyes, envied everyone to whom he spoke, had scarcely patience enough to help anybody to coffee; and then was enraged against herself for being so silly!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “enrage”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Tending to draw the attention or affections
vocabulary.context: I am perfectly satisfied from what his manners now are, that he never had any design of engaging my affection.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “engaging”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: With exposure to popular view or notice
vocabulary.context: It will then be publicly seen, that on both sides, we meet only as common and indifferent acquaintance.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “publicly”: -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To stop or pause respecting decision or action
vocabulary.context: On entering the room, he seemed to hesitate; but Jane happened to look round, and happened to smile: it was decided.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “hesitate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bennet, in the meanwhile, was giving way to all the happy schemes, which the good humour, and common politeness of Bingley, in half an hour’s visit, had revived.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “revive”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + viv (Latin vivere, "to live"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Seating at dinner revealed intentions and status.

discussionQuestions: Why is Jane insisting she is indifferent?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LIV,” how does Austen show renewed hope? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LIV develops the idea of renewed hope. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LIV to complicate the reader's understanding of renewed hope. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of renewed hope responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of renewed hope. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

options: To give strength or ability to

satQuestions.passage: “Now,” said she, “that this first meeting is over, I feel perfectly easy. I know my own strength, and I shall never be embarrassed again by his coming. I am glad he dines here on Tuesday. It will then be publicly seen, that on both sides, we meet only as common and indifferent acquaintance.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter LIV”?
options: Obsession and the discovery of life

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: “Now,” said she, “that this first meeting is over, I feel perfectly easy. I know my own strength, and I shall never be embarrassed again by his coming. I am glad he dines here on Tuesday. It will then be publicly seen, that on both sides, we meet only as common and indifferent acquaintance.”

annotationFocus.label: Plot
annotationFocus.lookFor: key events and the causes linking them

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why is Jane insisting she is indifferent? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are partridges, detaining, enabling, venison, roasted. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Darcy acknowledged, that the partridges were remarkably well done; and I suppose he has two or three French cooks at least.” Webster's says: Any one of numerous species of small gallinaceous birds of the genus Perdix and several related genera of the family…. Now the word history: “partridge”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “detain”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + tain (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “enable”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Seating at dinner revealed intentions and status. Why does this chapter matter? Restraint and miscommunication delay resolution. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to renewed hope.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Plot, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “Now,” said she, “that this first meeting is over, I feel perfectly easy. I know my own strength, and I shall never be embarrassed again by his coming. I am glad he dines here on Tuesday. It will then be publicly seen, that on both sides, we meet only as common and indifferent acquaintance.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Plot, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LIV,” how does Austen show renewed hope? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about renewed hope, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes renewed hope. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
